[T5](t5_interventions.qmd) showed how to vaccinate a group and change a parameter from a date. This tutorial covers interventions that reach particular people because of what has happened to them: treating people who seek care, screening and treating those who test positive, notifying their partners, and vaccinating people as they reach an age. These depend on individuals' infections, test results, and partners, so they run as agents.

## Products and interventions

Starsim has _products_ (the test, treatment, or vaccine itself) and _interventions_ (deliveries) that deliver them to people. There are three basic products, `ss.Vaccine`, `ss.Diagnostic`, and `ss.Treatment`, and a delivery for each: `ss.vaccinate()`, `ss.screen()`, and `ss.treat()`. A delivery says who receives the product (`who=`, including people as they reach an age, `ss.at_age()`), when (`when=`: times, how often, an event that has happened to them, or `ss.schedule()`), and how many (`coverage=`, `capacity=`). They rarely need tailoring to a disease, but you can write your own (see [A5](a5_modules.qmd)).

## Starting point

Measles has no treatment, so this tutorial uses the sexually transmitted infection from [A2](a2_networks.qmd): a simplified curable bacterial infection, like gonorrhea, that lasts 6 months on average untreated and leaves no immunity (SIS), on a sexual network of partnerships lasting about a month. Only 15% of people take part in the network (`participation=`): a core group with many short partnerships, where the infection is concentrated, as gonorrhea is. The network remembers partnerships for a year after they end (`memory=`), for partner notification. Births and deaths turn the population over, so people age into the groups interventions reach. It runs as 10,000 agents for 20 years, in monthly steps:

```{python}
import numpy as np
import starsim as ss

S, I = ss.states('S I')
infection = S >> I @ ss.peract(m2f=0.1, f2m=0.05)*I  # Chance of infection per act
recovery  = I >> S @ ss.months(6)                    # Infected for 6 months on average, untreated
sti = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.05)

settings = dict(
    networks     = ss.SexualNet(dur=ss.months(1), memory=ss.years(1), participation=ss.bernoulli(0.15)), # Partnerships of about a month, remembered for a year, among 15% of people
    demographics = [ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(0.02)), ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.02))],
    n_agents     = 10_000,
    start        = 2000,
    stop         = 2020,
    dt           = ss.months(1),
    verbose      = 0,
)
sim = ss.Sim(sti, **settings)
sim.run()
sim.plot('sti.I')
```

The infection is endemic, with about 6% of people infected, nearly all in the network. It takes a few years to settle, since many of those infected at the start are outside the network, and recover without passing it on.

## Treating people who seek care

Suppose 30% of people notice symptoms and seek care within about a month of infection, and are treated with a drug that cures 95%. The drug is the product; `ss.treat()` delivers it. `when=ss.on(sti.infection, delay=...)` delivers it to people a time after their infection, drawn for each person, and `coverage=0.3` to 30% of them:

```{python}
drug = ss.Treatment(cure=0.95) # Cures 95% of the people it is given to
care = ss.treat(drug, when=ss.on(sti.infection, delay=ss.uniform(ss.weeks(1), ss.months(2))), coverage=0.3)
```

The treatment is given when due, whether or not the person is still infected; for someone already recovered, it does nothing.

## Screening, and treating those who test positive

People without symptoms can only be found by screening. Here people aged 15 to 29, who have the most partners, are screened every 6 months from 2010, with a test that finds 90% of infections (sensitivity) and gives a false positive for 2% of the uninfected (specificity). Half of those eligible are reached in each round, and those who test positive (`screening.positive`) are treated. Written out, who is eligible is a function of the sim returning their UIDs, and when is a list of dates:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
young = (ss.person.age >= 15) & (ss.person.age < 30) # Who is eligible: a condition on each person, worked out when it is needed
screening = ss.screen(sensitivity=0.9, specificity=0.98, who=young, when=ss.schedule(every=ss.months(6), start='2010'), coverage=0.5)
treatment = ss.treat(drug, when=screening.positive)
```

## R

```r
drug <- ss$Treatment(cure = 0.95) # As above: cures 95% of the people it is given to
young <- (ss$person$age >= 15) & (ss$person$age < 30) # Who is eligible: a condition on each person, worked out when it is needed
screening <- ss$screen(sensitivity = 0.9, specificity = 0.98, who = young, when = ss$schedule(every = ss$months(6), start = "2010"), coverage = 0.5)
treatment <- ss$treat(drug, when = screening$positive)
```

## Explicit

```{python}
def young_people(sim):
    """ The UIDs of the people aged 15 to 29 """
    age = sim.people.age
    return age.auids[(age.values >= 15) & (age.values < 30)]

rounds = [f'{year}-{month}-01' for year in range(2010, 2020) for month in ['01', '07']] + ['2020-01-01'] # Every 6 months from 2010, to the end of the sim
screening = ss.screen(sensitivity=0.9, specificity=0.98, who=young_people, when=rounds, coverage=0.5)
treatment = ss.treat(drug, when=screening.positive)
```
:::

`who=` takes any condition on people or on a module's states, combined with `&` (and), `|` (or), and `~` (not): e.g. `young & ~sti.I` would screen only young people who aren't infected.

## Notifying partners

A person who tests positive was infected by someone, and may have infected others. With `trace=`, a delivery reaches the contacts, on the named network, of the people selected by `when=`; since the network remembers partnerships for a year, this includes past partners. Here half the partners of those who test positive are treated without testing (as in expedited partner therapy):

```{python}
notification = ss.treat(drug, when=screening.positive, coverage=0.5, trace='sexualnet')
```

Now compare these, each scenario adding one more intervention to the last:

```{python}
scenarios = {
    'No treatment':             [],
    'Treatment when seeking care': [care],
    'And screening':            [care, screening, treatment],
    'And partner notification': [care, screening, treatment, notification],
}
sims = {label: ss.Sim(sti, interventions=interventions, **settings) for label, interventions in scenarios.items()}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('sti.I')
```

Treating people who seek care cuts the number infected by about a third. Screening cuts it further, and notifying partners further still: each finds infections the others miss. The summary gives total infections over 20 years in each scenario:

```{python}
msim.summarize().loc['sti_infection']
```

The deliveries have results of their own, such as the numbers screened, positive, and partners treated:

```{python}
sim = msim.sims['And partner notification']
print('Screened:', sim.results.screening.delivered.sum())
print('Tested positive:', sim.results.screening.positive.sum())
print('Treated after testing positive:', sim.results.treatment.delivered.sum())
print('... of whom cured:', sim.results.treatment.cured.sum(), '- not cured:', sim.results.treatment.failed.sum(), '- not infected:', sim.results.treatment.unneeded.sum())
print('Partners treated:', sim.results.notification.delivered.sum())
```

About half of those treated after a positive test weren't infected: with only a few percent infected, even a 98% specific test gives about as many false positives as true ones. A treatment's outcomes, `cured`, `failed` (infected, not cured), and `unneeded` (not infected), are results and events: `ss.treat(..., when=treatment.failed)` would give a second-line drug, and resistance can be a transition triggered by `treatment.failed` (see [Products](../user_guide/interventions_products.qmd#treatment-outcomes-and-resistance)). Partner notification treats about twice as many people as screening finds, since each person who tests positive has had several partners in the past year, many of them infected.

## Individual histories

As agents, every delivery remembers for each person whether its event happened to them (`.ever`), how many times (`.n_times`), and how long ago (`.since`), e.g. how many times each person tested positive:

```{python}
screening = sim.interventions.screening
times_positive = screening.positive.n_times.values
print('Number of people who tested positive 0, 1, 2, ... times:', np.bincount(times_positive.astype(int)))
```

About a quarter of those who tested positive did so more than once, since a cure doesn't protect against the next infection: a reason to retest some months after treatment. A history can decide who receives something: `who=screening.positive.since <= ss.months(6)` reaches people who tested positive in the past 6 months (e.g. for a retest), and `who=~treatment.ever` people never treated.

## Vaccination as people reach an age

There is no gonorrhea vaccine in routine use, but a meningococcal vaccine appears to give some protection, perhaps 30–40%. Suppose one 35% effective is given to 80% of people as they turn 15, from 2010. `ss.at_age()` is routine delivery as people reach an age: each person is offered it once, on the step they reach it (not everyone older on the first day). Reaching everyone at risk this way takes decades, so these runs go to 2040:

```{python}
vaccination = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.35, who=ss.at_age(15), start='2010', coverage=0.8)

long = dict(settings, stop=2040) # 40 years instead of 20
sims = {
    'Treatment when seeking care': ss.Sim(sti, interventions=care, **long),
    'And vaccination at age 15':   ss.Sim(sti, interventions=[care, vaccination], **long),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('sti.I')
print('Doses:', msim.sims['And vaccination at age 15'].results.vaccination.delivered.sum())
```

The vaccine makes little difference for ten years, and by 2040 lowers prevalence by about a quarter: here people have partners at any age after debut, so vaccinated cohorts replace unvaccinated ones only as the population turns over, and protection is partial. Where infection is concentrated in the young, vaccination at 15 works much sooner. By default a vaccine is leaky: everyone vaccinated is 35% less likely to be infected at each exposure. With `leaky=False` it is all or nothing (35% fully protected), and `waning=` makes protection fade; see [Products](../user_guide/interventions_products.qmd).

## Interventions of your own

These deliveries cover most programs. For a rule of your own, `who=` takes a function of the sim that returns UIDs, as in the screening above; an intervention that does something no product does is a module written as code, a class with a `step()` method. [T9](t9_modules.qmd) and [A5](a5_modules.qmd) show how, and [Interventions](../user_guide/interventions_interventions.qmd) in the user guide covers the rest: capacity, priority, queues, and delays.

## Exercises

1. In the scenario with partner notification, what happens if the partners of people who seek care are notified too (a second notification, with `when=care`)? Is the effect larger than notifying the partners of those found by screening?
2. Screening reaches people aged 15 to 29. How much does the effect change if it reaches everyone aged 15 to 49 instead, and how many more tests does it take? Which gives more infections prevented per test?
3. Add a catch-up campaign to the vaccination at age 15: a single round in 2010 (`when=['2010']`) for everyone aged 15 to 29, with the same vaccine. How much sooner does vaccination make a difference, and how many more doses does it take?
